Consult Summary:
- Adult patient with known asthma presents with 2–3 days of exertional shortness of breath, wheeze, and cough. Blue inhaler (salbutamol) provides little relief; patient has been using inhalers daily for prevention. Plan includes urgent assessment today, adjustment of controller therapy, and close follow-up with a GP within a few days; potential antibiotics/steroids if indicated after exam; advised to seek A&E if symptoms worsen.

- Note: There is a conflicting statement in the record: patient reports hay fever (allergic rhinitis) as an allergy, while the clinician states “no allergies.” This conflict is documented in the Allergies section.

Problem List:

Issue 1:
- Acute asthma exacerbation presenting with 2–3 days of shortness of breath on exertion (running), wheeze, and cough; currently using blue inhaler (salbutamol) with inadequate relief; using inhaler daily for prevention as well.
- Associated features: no productive cough reported; no fever noted; no hospital admission previously for asthma; last asthma attack 3–4 years ago.
- Respiratory history: history of eczema; possible seasonal allergic rhinitis (hay fever) mentioned by patient.
- Functional status: normal peak flow at baseline reported previously (approximately 380 L/min).
- Physical exam: chest exam not yet performed; peak flow measurement planned today.
- Plan: GP appointment within the next few days; increase brown inhaler (Clenil/beclometasone) from 3 puffs twice daily to 4 puffs twice daily; continue salbutamol as needed, potentially up to every 2 hours (advised maximum 2–4 hours). If breathing worsens or patient has frequent use without improvement, proceed to A&E. Perform chest exam and peak flow today; may consider antibiotics and steroids if indicated by exam. Schedule follow-up with a GP; consider face-to-face appointment.

Issue 2:
- History of eczema; currently managed with topical hydrocortisone and Cetraben (emollient). 
- Plan: Continue current topical regimen; monitor as part of overall asthma management.

Issue 3:
- Self-reported hay fever (seasonal allergic rhinitis).
- Plan: No specific changes documented beyond acknowledgement; allergy to medications not reported.

Medications:
- Salbutamol inhaler (blue inhaler) – use as needed; currently used daily for prevention and during symptoms; frequency advised up to every 2–4 hours as needed.
- Beclometasone inhaler (brown inhaler; referred to as Clenil) – current dose 3 puffs twice daily; plan to increase to 4 puffs twice daily.
- Hydrocortisone (topical) – dose not documented.
- Cetraben (emollient) – dose not documented.
- Bactroban (topical antibiotic) – dose not documented (listed as “Flanel Bactroban” in transcript; exact formulation unclear).

Allergies:
- Hay fever (seasonal allergic rhinitis) reported by patient.
- No drug allergies reported (clinician stated “no allergies” in conversation, which conflicts with patient’s hay fever note).

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.
- Eczema.
- Hay fever/allergic rhinitis (patient-reported).
- No prior asthma-related hospitalizations; last asthma attack 3–4 years ago.
- Last asthma review with nurse about two years ago.

Social History:
- Not documented (no information provided about smoking, alcohol, living situation beyond address).

Preventative History:
- Not documented.

Physical Examination:
- No vitals provided.
- Chest examination planned; peak flow measurement to be performed during the visit.

Plan:
- Arrange GP follow-up in next few days; airway status to be reviewed.
- Increase brown inhaler (beclometasone) to 4 puffs twice daily.
- Continue salbutamol inhaler as needed; up to every 2 hours if necessary, with the goal to avoid frequent use.
- If breathing worsens or frequent blue inhaler use persists, go to A&E.
- Perform chest exam and peak flow today to guide further management; possible need for antibiotics and steroids if indicated by findings.
- Schedule a follow-up (face-to-face) after the assessment with the GP.
- Interim support: book call support; arrange appointment.

Quality checks:
- Missing elements: Vitals (no numbers), full medication reconciliation with doses/routes/frequencies, smoking/alcohol history, and comprehensive preventive health data (immunizations, screenings) are not documented.
- Conflicts: Hay fever noted as an allergy by patient but denied by clinician; conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Some confusion in medication naming (Flanel Bactroban vs Bactroban; Cetraben/Hydrocortisone discussion). Overall content adequate but phrasing is inconsistent; clinical plan remains coherent.
